replies.text: Settled by your note: Accepted. 'finish' is your later command. The removal step cannot delete the feature worktree and the local feature branch, because the session that runs gc has that folder as its working folder (record 0002). So the removal deletes the run worktree, the run branch and the remote feature branch, and leaves those 2. After you close the session, finish deletes the feature worktree folder, then the local feature branch, then the target file.

Settled by your note: Accepted. The lease: gc tells the forge 'delete this branch only if it still points at commit X', where X is the tip gc checked. If someone pushed a new commit to the branch after the check, the forge refuses the delete, so that new commit is not lost. gc then reports it as a failed delete. Git calls this --force-with-lease.

The target file carries what gc listed from the list step, which runs in the feature worktree, to the removal and to your later command. Your command runs after the session closes, maybe from the main checkout, so it must not guess its target from the folder it runs in (grill decision i-target). It lives until your later command ends with nothing left, and that command deletes it. Round 3 asks this again as one card.

A change that merges long after the agents stopped: nothing tells anyone, because an idle agent receives no event (PRD, the trigger decision). You run /afkv2:gc yourself when you come back (user story 2). An agent that later runs the CI watch or mark-ready on that change offers gc too. Your README request is a scope question, so round 3 asks it as a fork.

A change that is still open, with a failed job or a conflict: gc refuses it as 'not merged' and removes nothing. Fixing it is the work of create-change-request, not of gc. A merged change cannot have a conflict any more. The contract does not change, but a note returns a sign-off, so round 3 asks for your sign again.

Over 100 changes from one source branch happens only on a long-lived branch that is merged again and again, for example a develop branch with one change per release over years. A feature branch has 1 or 2. Refusing is the safe side, because gc cannot prove that none of the unread changes is open. The contract does not change; round 3 asks for your sign again.

Agreed. I checked the Windows errors on this machine: a folder used as working folder gives error 32, a process in a subfolder or a file held open gives error 5 (the same code as a missing right), a taken name gives 183, and a folder already gone gives 2. Round 3 shows the new rule rows for your sign.
